books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, A. Political Parties and the Rise of the First Two-Party System

stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson, Notes on the State of Virginia, Query XIX (written 1781-82, first published in English 1787), public domain. Abridged.
stimulus.text:
“Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, if ever he had a chosen people, whose breasts he has made his peculiar deposit for substantial and genuine virtue. It is the focus in which he keeps alive that sacred fire, which otherwise might escape from the face of the earth.”
— Thomas Jefferson, Notes on the State of Virginia, Query XIX (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia (1787)
stem: The vision in the passage best explains Jefferson's opposition to Hamilton's economic program because Hamilton's program would

options.text: give western land away to settlers for almost nothing
options.misconception: Cheap western land was Jefferson's own policy, not Hamilton's; Hamilton's program centered on finance and manufacturing.

options.text: build a commercial society of banks and factories that would corrupt virtue
keep the national government weak and leave power with the states
options.misconception: A weak national government was Jefferson's own wish, not Hamilton's plan.

options.text: end all foreign trade and close American ports
options.misconception: Hamilton wanted to grow American trade and manufacturing, not to end trade.

rationales.A: Cheap western land was Jefferson's own policy, not Hamilton's. Hamilton's program centered on finance and manufacturing.
rationales.B: Jefferson believed virtue lived in the independent farmer, and Hamilton's bank, tariffs, and factories would raise up the opposite America: merchants, bankers, and wage workers crowded into cities. Background: Jefferson warned elsewhere that the mobs of great cities add to pure government what sores add to the strength of the body, so Hamilton's program struck at the very citizen his passage honors.
rationales.C: A weak national government was Jefferson's own wish, not Hamilton's plan.
rationales.D: Hamilton wanted to grow American trade and manufacturing, not to end trade.
rationales.general:
1. Name Jefferson's ideal. The independent farmer, whose virtue keeps the republic honest.
2. Name Hamilton's program. A national bank, tariffs, and government-backed manufacturing.
3. Ask what that program builds. Cities, commerce, and wage labor, the opposite of the farming republic.
4. Put it together. Jefferson opposed Hamilton because the program would breed the citizens he feared.
Remember: a policy fight is often a fight over what kind of person the country should produce.
